nodes.label: Mountain clothing
nodes.answer: Always use appropriate clothing in layers. Choose moisture-wicking base layers, insulating mid layers, and a wind- and water-resistant shell so you can adjust to changing temperature, wind, rain, and exertion.

nodes.label: Layering system
nodes.answer: Use a base layer to move sweat away from your skin, a mid layer to retain warmth, and an outer shell to block wind and precipitation. Add or remove layers during activity and rest stops to avoid overheating or chilling.

nodes.label: Base layer
nodes.answer: Wear a close-fitting base layer made from merino wool or synthetic fabric to wick sweat and keep skin dry. Avoid cotton next to the skin because it absorbs moisture, dries slowly, and can make you cold.

nodes.label: Mid layer
nodes.answer: Use a fleece, softshell, or insulated jacket as a mid layer to trap warm air. Choose synthetic insulation for damp conditions, and add it during breaks, on exposed ridges, or when temperatures fall.

nodes.label: Outer shell
nodes.answer: Carry a breathable waterproof and windproof shell for rain, snow, and wind. A hood, adjustable cuffs, pit zips or vents, and compatible shell trousers make it much more useful in mountain conditions.

nodes.label: Hiking trousers
nodes.answer: Choose quick-drying, stretchy hiking trousers with good freedom of movement. In cold or wet weather, add thermal leggings underneath and waterproof overtrousers rather than relying on one heavy pair of trousers.

nodes.label: Gloves and mittens
nodes.answer: Carry gloves suited to the forecast, plus a spare dry pair. Use thin liner gloves for dexterity and warmer insulated or waterproof gloves for cold, wind, rain, or snow.

nodes.label: Headwear
nodes.answer: Bring both sun protection and warmth for your head: a wide-brimmed or peaked hat in sunny weather and a beanie or buff for cold, wind, and rain. A large proportion of body heat can be lost through an unprotected head in cold conditions.

nodes.label: Footwear
nodes.answer: Choose footwear for the terrain, season, and load: flexible trail shoes for dry paths, supportive boots for rough or rocky ground, and insulated or crampon-compatible boots for winter terrain. Keep footwear dry and carry spare socks.

nodes.label: Socks
nodes.answer: Wear well-fitting hiking socks made from wool or a synthetic blend, and carry at least one spare dry pair. Avoid cotton socks, which stay wet and increase the risk of blisters and cold feet.

nodes.label: Rainwear
nodes.answer: Use a waterproof jacket and trousers when sustained rain is likely. Keep spare clothing and electronics in dry bags, and prioritize ventilation to reduce sweat buildup inside waterproofs.

nodes.label: Winter clothing
nodes.answer: For winter mountain travel, carry more insulation than you expect to need, protect extremities, and keep a dry set of clothes for emergencies. Wet clothing loses insulation, so manage sweat and precipitation carefully.

nodes.label: Summer clothing
nodes.answer: In summer, choose lightweight, breathable clothing that protects against sun and abrasion. Even in warm weather, carry a light insulating layer and rain shell for sudden mountain weather changes.

nodes.label: Spare clothing
nodes.answer: Pack a dry base layer, warm hat, gloves, socks, and an insulating layer in a waterproof bag. Dry spare clothing is essential if you get wet, delayed, injured, or caught in worsening weather.

nodes.label: Clothing materials
nodes.answer: Merino wool and synthetic fabrics are usually better than cotton for active mountain use because they manage moisture more effectively. Down is very warm when dry, while synthetic insulation continues to insulate better when damp.

nodes.label: Adjusting layers
nodes.answer: Start slightly cool, ventilate while moving uphill, and add insulation immediately at rest stops, summits, or exposed sections. Removing a layer before you overheat helps prevent sweat from chilling you later.

nodes.label: Sun protection clothing
nodes.answer: Use long sleeves, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen for high UV exposure. Protection matters more at altitude and around snow, where reflected sunlight can be intense.

nodes.label: Wind protection
nodes.answer: Use a wind-resistant shell on exposed ridges, summits, and cold descents. Blocking wind reduces wind chill and helps preserve the insulation provided by your other layers.

nodes.label: Moisture management
nodes.answer: Stay dry by ventilating during hard effort, changing out of wet clothing promptly, and keeping spare layers in waterproof bags. Wet clothing loses insulation and substantially increases the risk of hypothermia.

nodes.label: Mountain clothing packing list
nodes.answer: For a mountain day trip, carry a moisture-wicking base layer, insulating mid layer, waterproof shell, suitable trousers, gloves, hat, spare socks, and dry emergency clothing. Adjust the list for season, forecast, route exposure, and trip length.
